passage:
I'm Kalyani, and I work at the toy shop in the market. On Saturday a little boy, Arnab, came in with his grandfather, who told him, "Pick any one toy."
Arnab walked down our long aisle of cars, dolls, puzzles and balls. He picked up a truck, put it down, touched a drum. Then he stood in the middle and started to cry. I can't say what he was thinking.
His grandfather knelt and held up just two things: a red truck and a small drum. "This or this?"
Arnab grabbed the truck and hugged it all the way to the counter.

qa.q: What two toys did Arnab's grandfather hold up?
qa.a: A red truck and a small drum.

qa.q: Why might Arnab have started to cry in the middle of the aisle?
qa.a: With so many cars, dolls, puzzles and balls, every choice may have felt too big, and not knowing which one to pick could have upset him. 😢

qa.q: Which choice by the grandfather turned things around, and why?
qa.a: Holding up just two toys, because a small choice was easy for Arnab to make and he could feel happy with it.

qa.q: How does Kalyani see the scene?
qa.a: Kalyani watches from the shop, sees the crying and then the happy hug, and admits not knowing what Arnab was thinking.

grounding: A shop worker describes a young child who is overwhelmed by a long aisle of toys but chooses happily from two.

passage:
Saturday: At the big toy fair, Zainab's aunt Aditi said, "Choose one!" Zainab stared at walls of toys, touched ten things, then sat on the floor and cried. They left with nothing.
Tuesday: At home, Aditi put just three things on the bed: a ball, a puzzle, a doll. "Which one for today?" Zainab picked the puzzle at once and did it twice.
The next Saturday: At a tiny toy shop near the mosque, Aditi asked the shopkeeper to show three small toys only. Zainab looked, chose the wooden bird, and skipped out holding it high.

qa.q: What did Zainab choose at the tiny toy shop?
qa.a: Zainab chose the wooden bird.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling at the big toy fair, and what shows it?
qa.a: Zainab seemed overwhelmed and upset; she touched ten things, then sat on the floor and cried.

qa.q: What was Aditi's turning point, and why did it help?
qa.a: On Tuesday Aditi offered only three things, which let Zainab choose easily, so she used the same idea at the shop.

qa.q: What might Aditi have felt leaving the toy fair with nothing?
qa.a: Aditi may have felt puzzled and a bit sad, since she meant the big choice as a treat and it ended in tears.

grounding: Shows over a week how a young child freezes before too many toys but chooses happily from three.

passage:
The toy shop in the mall was closing in ten minutes, and Indu had only two hundred rupees left for her son's birthday gift. "Anything from this wall, Vaibhav," she said.
The wall was huge: cars, robots, bubble guns, puzzles, balls. Vaibhav reached for a robot, then a car, then a ball, and froze, his lip trembling. The lights started switching off at the back. "Quick, quick," Indu said.
Vaibhav began to wail and grabbed the nearest thing, a plastic whistle.
At home he blew it once and dropped it. Next time, Indu thought, she'd pick three toys and let him choose.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav grab in the end?
qa.a: Vaibhav grabbed the nearest thing, a plastic whistle.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav freeze in front of the wall?
qa.a: So many cars, robots and balls, plus the rush, made each choice feel uncertain, and he couldn't settle on one.

qa.q: What plan does Indu make, and why is it likely to work?
qa.a: She plans to pick three toys and let him choose, because a small set is easier for a young child and he may enjoy what he picks.

qa.q: What was the rush like for Indu?
qa.a: Indu had little money and ten minutes, and her 'Quick, quick' shows how stressed she was as the lights went off.

grounding: Shows a young child who, facing a huge wall of toys under time pressure, freezes, cries and grabs the nearest item.

passage: Seema Masi took Leela to the new toy shop near their Pune colony. "Choose anything you like!" The shelves went up to the ceiling: dolls, trains, kites, clay, puzzles, drums. Leela picked up a kite, put it back, touched a train, looked at the dolls. Her lip began to wobble. She grabbed the rubber ball nearest the counter and held it tight. At home she pushed it under the sofa. The next week Masi put just three things on the mat: clay, a puzzle and a kite. Leela chose the clay and made snakes all evening.

qa.q: What did Leela grab in the toy shop?
qa.a: The rubber ball nearest the counter.

qa.q: What does Leela's wobbling lip suggest she was feeling in the big shop?
qa.a: It suggests she felt overwhelmed and upset, because every toy looked possible and she couldn't settle on one 😢

qa.q: What did Seema Masi change the next week, and why did it work?
qa.a: She put just three things on the mat, so choosing felt easy and Leela was happy with the clay all evening.

qa.q: What might Seema Masi have felt when Leela pushed the ball under the sofa?
qa.a: She may have felt puzzled or a little disappointed, since she had offered anything at all and Leela still didn't enjoy her pick.

grounding: A young child faced with shelves of toys freezes, nearly cries and grabs the nearest one, but enjoys choosing from three.

passage:
"Papa, I want... that one. No, that one!" Chaitanya's finger jumped from robot to truck to drum.
"Take your time," said Lalit, his father.
"There's too much!" Chaitanya sat down on the shop floor, eyes wet.
Lalit crouched beside him. "Okay. Let's make it small. Close your eyes." He took three toys off the shelf: a red truck, a drum and a robot. "Open. Only these three."
Chaitanya looked. He touched the truck. "This one."
"Sure?"
"Yes! Vroom!" He zoomed it along Papa's knee, all the way to the counter.

qa.q: Which three toys did Lalit take off the shelf?
qa.a: A red truck, a drum and a robot.

qa.q: What does Chaitanya sitting on the floor with wet eyes suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He felt swamped and frustrated, because there were too many toys and he couldn't pick one.

qa.q: What choice did Lalit make that turned things around?
qa.a: Instead of hurrying him or leaving, he cut the choice down to three toys, which made picking quick and left Chaitanya happy with the truck.

qa.q: What might that moment on the shop floor have been like for Lalit?
qa.a: He may have felt a mix of worry and patience, wanting his son to enjoy the treat rather than end it in tears.

grounding: A father sees his young son freeze and cry among too many toys and makes choosing easy by offering only three.

passage:
Saturday. For her fifth birthday, Neelam masi took Binita to the huge toy shop in the mall. Aisles and aisles. Binita walked up and down, touching everything, then stood in the middle and burst into tears. Masi carried her out with nothing.
Wednesday. Binita kept asking about the shop, but hid behind Masi's leg when she said they could go back.
The next Sunday. Masi put three toys on the bed at home: a skipping rope, a doll and a puzzle. "One is yours." Binita looked for a minute, chose the puzzle, and hugged it all evening.

qa.q: Which three toys did Masi put on the bed?
qa.a: A skipping rope, a doll and a puzzle.

qa.q: Why did Binita burst into tears in the huge toy shop?
qa.a: Binita felt overwhelmed by aisles and aisles of toys, so choosing just one felt impossible.

qa.q: What did Masi do differently the next Sunday, and why did it work?
qa.a: She offered only three toys at home, a small choice that Binita could manage and feel happy with.

qa.q: How might Neelam masi have felt carrying Binita out with nothing?
qa.a: Masi probably felt disappointed and puzzled, having planned a happy birthday trip, which led her to try a smaller choice.

grounding: Shows a young child freezing and crying among too many toys, then choosing happily from just three.

passage: The Dussehra fair was closing, rain was starting, and Santosh told his son, "Akash, one toy, quickly!" The stall had hundreds: cars, drums, masks, balloons, spinning tops. Akash's eyes darted everywhere. The shopkeeper was pulling down the plastic sheet. "Quick, beta!" Akash grabbed the nearest thing, a tin whistle, and held it tight. All the way home on the scooter he sat silent. At home he threw the whistle on the floor. "I wanted the drum," he sobbed. Santosh sighed and picked it up. Next year, he thought, he'd ask Akash at home to choose between a drum and a car, before they even left.

qa.q: What did Akash grab from the stall?
qa.a: Akash grabbed a tin whistle.

qa.q: Why did Akash throw the whistle on the floor at home?
qa.a: Akash felt disappointed and upset; rushed among hundreds of toys, he had grabbed the nearest one instead of the drum he really wanted.

qa.q: What is Santosh's plan for next year, and why is it better?
qa.a: Asking Akash at home to choose between just a drum and a car, so there are few options and no rush.

qa.q: How might Santosh have felt on the scooter ride home?
qa.a: Santosh might have felt tired and a little guilty about rushing Akash at a crowded stall.

grounding: Shows a young child rushed among too many toys grabbing the nearest one and feeling unhappy later.

passage: In the toy shop on Commercial Street, Shankar, four, stood frozen in front of a wall of toy cars. Police jeeps, fire engines, racing cars with doors that opened. He picked one up, put it down, picked up another, then sat on the floor and started to whimper. His big brother Abhinav crouched beside him. "Okay. Just these two," he said, holding up a fire engine and a yellow racing car. "Which one?" Shankar looked from one to the other. Only two. He pointed at the fire engine. On the way home he made siren noises the whole auto ride, grinning.

qa.q: Which two cars did Abhinav hold up?
qa.a: A fire engine and a yellow racing car.

qa.q: Why did Shankar sit on the floor and whimper?
qa.a: Shankar felt overwhelmed by the wall of cars, so picking one felt too hard.

qa.q: What did Abhinav do that helped, and why did it work?
qa.a: He narrowed the choice to just two cars, which Shankar could easily compare and choose between.

qa.q: How might Abhinav have felt hearing the siren noises on the way home?
qa.a: Abhinav probably felt pleased and proud that a simple trick made his little brother so happy.

grounding: Shows a young child freezing in front of too many toy cars and choosing happily once given only two.

qa.q: How might Imran have felt watching Sahil beat the drum all the way home?

passage:
Diwali fair visit, note by the class teacher.

At the school's Diwali fair, Irawati stood at the toy table for a long time. There were balloons, clay animals, puzzles and bangles. She picked up a puzzle, dropped it, grabbed a whistle, then started to cry and held her friend Uma's hand tightly.

I moved most things aside and left out two clay animals and a small puzzle. Irawati chose the clay elephant within a minute and showed it to everyone. Next fair I will set out small baskets with fewer toys for the little ones. 🪔

qa.q: What did Irawati choose after the table was cleared?
qa.a: She chose the clay elephant within a minute.

qa.q: Why did Irawati start to cry at the toy table?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed by all the balloons, clay animals, puzzles and bangles, and couldn't settle on one.

qa.q: What change does the teacher plan for the next fair?
qa.a: The teacher plans small baskets with fewer toys so the little ones can choose more easily.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Uma when Irawati held her hand tightly?
qa.a: Uma may have felt worried for her friend or unsure what to do, then happy when Irawati cheered up.

grounding: A teacher notes a young child freezing and crying at a crowded toy table and choosing happily from a small selection.

passage:
It was the Pongal fair in the village, and the air smelled of sugarcane. Nitin's grandmother Lakshmi gave him ten rupees for the toy stall. The man had whistles, tin frogs, clay pots, balloons and wooden tops piled high.

Nitin looked left and right. He grabbed the nearest balloon, then shook his head and pushed it back. His eyes filled.

Paati Lakshmi picked two things: a tin frog and a wooden top. "Which one, kanna?"

Nitin took the frog and clicked it all the way to the bullock cart.

qa.q: How much money did Lakshmi give Nitin for the toy stall?
qa.a: She gave him ten rupees.

qa.q: Why did Nitin's eyes fill at the stall?
qa.a: He felt overwhelmed and upset because the pile of toys was so big that he couldn't decide and grabbed the nearest one.

qa.q: What did Paati Lakshmi do well to help Nitin?
qa.a: She narrowed it down to two things, so Nitin could make a choice that made him happy.

qa.q: How might the stall owner see a child who grabs and then returns a toy?
qa.a: The stall owner may feel impatient or amused, since many small children get stuck in front of a crowded stall.

grounding: A young child at a village fair freezes and grabs at a crowded stall, then chooses happily when offered two toys.

passage:
It was the week before New Year, and the toy shop in Madrid was full of lights. Santiago told his little cousin Elif, "Pick one toy. Any one."
Elif looked left: dolls. Right: puzzles. Up: a wall of stuffed animals. Down: a hundred tiny cars.
She stood very still. Then her lip shook, and she started to cry.
Santiago crouched down. He picked three things: a bear, a puzzle and a red car. "Just these three. Which one?"
Elif stopped crying, looked carefully, and hugged the bear.

qa.q: How many things did Santiago pick for Elif to choose from?
qa.a: Santiago picked three things: a bear, a puzzle and a red car.

qa.q: Why did Elif start to cry in the toy shop?
qa.a: Elif felt overwhelmed by toys everywhere, so choosing just one felt impossible.

qa.q: Why did Santiago's idea work?
qa.a: Three toys were few enough for Elif to look at carefully and choose happily.

qa.q: How might Santiago have felt when Elif cried?
qa.a: Santiago was probably surprised and a bit worried, then relieved when the three-toy idea worked.

grounding: Shows a young child who freezes and cries in a toy shop full of choices, and chooses happily from a small selection.

In Puja week, the nursery class got a craft corner with a huge tray of stickers: stars, flowers, animals, letters, hundreds of them.
"Choose some for your card," said Saurabh Sir.
Binita stared at the tray. She touched a star, then a tiger, then a flower. Everyone else was sticking. She grabbed the nearest ones, three grey circles, and stuck them on crooked.
Then she looked at her card and burst into tears. "It's ugly!"
The next day, Saurabh Sir gave each child a small cup with just five stickers. Binita chose slowly, one by one, and smiled at her card.

qa.q: How many stickers were in each child's cup the next day?
qa.a: Each child got a small cup with just five stickers.

qa.q: Why did Binita grab the grey circles?
qa.a: Binita felt overwhelmed and rushed by the huge tray, so she grabbed the nearest ones without really choosing.

qa.q: Why did the small cups help Binita?
qa.a: With only five stickers, Binita could choose slowly and feel happy with her card.

qa.q: How might Saurabh Sir feel seeing Binita smile on the second day?
qa.a: Saurabh Sir probably feels pleased and relieved that the smaller choice helped.

grounding: Shows a young child who grabs the nearest stickers from a huge tray and is happier choosing from a few.

passage:
Saturday, the first hot week of summer. At the ice cream parlour, thirty flavours sat in the glass case. Kavitha pressed her nose to it and couldn't choose. The queue grew. She started to cry, and Nitin Chacha bought vanilla just to leave.
Wednesday. She pointed at the nearest tub without looking. It was coffee. She took one lick and made a face.
Sunday. Before they went in, Nitin Chacha said, "Today it's mango or chocolate. Only two."
Kavitha thought hard on the way. At the counter she said, "Mango!" She ate every drop.

qa.q: How many flavours were in the glass case?
qa.a: Thirty flavours sat in the glass case.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha cry on Saturday?
qa.a: Kavitha felt overwhelmed by thirty flavours and a growing queue, so she couldn't choose at all.

qa.q: What did Nitin Chacha do on Sunday, and why did it work?
qa.a: He offered only mango or chocolate before going in, giving Kavitha a small, easy choice.

qa.q: What was Saturday like for Nitin Chacha?
qa.a: Nitin Chacha was probably flustered by the tears and the queue, buying vanilla just to leave.

grounding: Shows a young child who freezes or grabs the nearest option when faced with many flavours, and enjoys choosing from two.

passage:
On the evening before Eid, the toy shop in the bazaar was packed, and the shopkeeper was already pulling down one shutter. "Ten minutes!" he called.
Afreen stood before a wall of dolls, cars, whistles and puzzles, clutching her Eidi. Her lip began to wobble. She picked up a car, put it back, touched a doll, and burst into tears.
Rekha Aunty crouched beside her and held up just three things. "Kite, tea set or ball?"
Afreen stopped crying, looked at each one, and hugged the tea set. She smiled all the way home.

qa.q: How many things did Rekha Aunty hold up?
qa.a: She held up just three things: a kite, a tea set and a ball.

qa.q: Why did Afreen burst into tears in front of the wall of toys?
qa.a: There were so many toys and so little time that she felt overwhelmed and could not settle on one.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Rekha Aunty holding up only three things worked, because Afreen could look at each one and choose calmly.

qa.q: What would change if Rekha Aunty had said, "Pick anything you like"?
qa.a: Afreen would probably keep crying or grab the nearest toy, and she might not feel as happy with it on the way home.

grounding: Shows a young child freezing and crying in front of too many toys, and choosing happily from a small selection.
